# The Voiceverse NFT Plagiarism Scandal

The Voiceverse NFT Plagiarism Scandal, which erupted in early 2022, stands as a seminal event in the history of the nascent Web3 and artificial intelligence industries. It was not merely an instance of intellectual property theft but a complex case study exposing deep-seated issues of haste, deception, and a lack of ethical governance within the burgeoning NFT ecosystem . The controversy centered on Voiceverse, a blockchain-based startup that marketed proprietary AI voice cloning technology sold as non-fungible tokens (NFTs) , . The scandal began when the project's creators were exposed for using a free, non-commercial text-to-speech service named 15.ai to generate promotional voice clips without permission or attribution , . To conceal their actions, they manipulated the audio files through pitch-shifting, attempting to pass off the stolen content as their own original technology , . This brazen act was swiftly uncovered through forensic evidence provided by the 15.ai developer, whose server logs irrefutably linked the infringing content to Voiceverse's promotional materials , . The incident transformed from a niche tech controversy into a mainstream media event following the involvement of prominent voice actor Troy Baker, whose controversial partnership announcement amplified the backlash , . His subsequent termination of the collaboration underscored the severity of the reputational damage inflicted upon Voiceverse , . The scandal did not occur in isolation; it was a symptom of a larger industry-wide plague of plagiarism that plagued major NFT marketplaces like OpenSea and Cent, where hundreds of thousands of fraudulent assets were being minted daily , . Furthermore, the investigation into Voiceverse extended beyond the initial incident to scrutinize its founder, artist Saba Moeel, revealing additional allegations of visual art tracing and the commodification of Black culture, leading to her censure by professional institutions like the Toronto Comic Arts Festival , . The long-term repercussions of the Voiceverse scandal proved profound, providing critical evidence in subsequent class-action lawsuits against Voiceverse's parent company, LOVO, Inc. , . These legal battles established new precedents, demonstrating that while traditional copyright law may be ill-equipped to handle AI-generated clones, state-level "right of publicity" laws and breach-of-contract claims offer powerful new avenues for holding companies accountable for deceptive data acquisition practices , . Thus, the Voiceverse scandal serves as a foundational case, illustrating how a single act of misconduct can ripple outward, shaping platform policies, influencing legal frameworks, and setting enduring standards for accountability in the digital age.

## The Deception Unveiled: A Timeline of Plagiarism and Exposure

The Voiceverse scandal unfolded over a ten-day period in January 2022, a timeline marked by premeditated deception, rapid discovery, and a series of contradictory corporate responses. The core of the incident involved the unauthorized use of creative work from the open-source, non-commercial AI research project 15.ai, which was then misrepresented as proprietary technology , . The sequence of events reveals a calculated attempt by the Voiceverse marketing team to create a high-impact demonstration for a major partnership announcement while simultaneously evading attribution and violating terms of service , . On January 4, 2022, just ten days before a highly anticipated partnership announcement, members of the Voiceverse team utilized 15.ai's text-to-speech platform to generate voice lines for characters from the popular animated series 'My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic' , . Specifically, they created the character lines "Hi Frens! We giggle in the Chubbiverse..." attributed to Twilight Sparkle and "Hi Frens! i got an alpha drop for you?!?" attributed to Rainbow Dash , . This initial act constituted a direct violation of 15.ai's terms of service, which explicitly prohibited commercial use and required mandatory attribution for any derivative works , . In an effort to hide their theft, the Voiceverse team employed a technical maneuver: they applied pitch-shifting to the generated audio files , , . This manipulation was designed to alter the vocal characteristics enough to make the origin less obvious, allowing them to falsely market the clips as their own proprietary AI voice cloning technology in promotional animations for their "Chubbiverse" project , . This act of misrepresentation was central to the deception, framing a clear-cut case of plagiarism as an innovative technological achievement.

The meticulously crafted facade of innovation was shattered on January 14, 2022, when the pseudonymous creator of 15.ai publicly exposed the deception . Using irrefutable evidence from the 15.ai server logs, the developer demonstrated that Voiceverse had indeed used their service to generate the infringing content nine days prior to the public announcement . The server logs timestamped the generation of the exact audio files and directly correlated them with Voiceverse's promotional videos, which were themselves timestamped on January 4, 2022 . This forensic evidence left no room for plausible deniability, proving the theft occurred during a frantic rush to prepare a tech demo for the upcoming partnership announcement , . Within hours of this public revelation, Voiceverse issued a response. Initially, the company denied the allegations . However, this stance was quickly abandoned as the evidence mounted. At 2:09 p.m. EST on the same day, January 14, 2022, Voiceverse posted a public apology on Twitter , . The apology tweet read: "Hey @fifteenai we are extremely sorry about this. The voice was indeed taken from your platform, which our marketing team used without giving proper credit. Chubbiverse team has no knowledge of this. We will make sure this never happens again." . While acknowledging the wrongdoing, this statement attempted to mitigate responsibility by attributing the entire incident to a rogue "marketing team," thereby distancing the rest of the organization, specifically the "Chubbiverse team," from the act , . This narrative was a classic deflection tactic, suggesting a lack of internal oversight and accountability rather than a coordinated strategy of deception. The apology was met with further criticism, particularly because it came from a platform known for supporting NFT integration, a stance that had been opposed by the 15.ai developer since December 2021 .

The aftermath of the exposure saw a swift and decisive break from one of its most prominent figures. The partnership with voice actor Troy Baker, announced on January 14, became untenable. Despite the apology, the damage to Voiceverse's credibility was severe, and the company faced immediate community backlash upon its launch . The incident also cast a long shadow over the broader NFT market, which was already grappling with rampant fraud and plagiarism , . The Voiceverse case became a cautionary tale, cited in AI incident databases and by news outlets like Eurogamer and Kotaku Australia as a prime example of theft stemming from generative artificial intelligence . The scandal's legacy extended far beyond the initial apology, providing crucial evidence in future legal proceedings that would hold the company's parent entity accountable for similar patterns of misconduct , . The detailed timeline underscores a critical lesson for emerging tech companies: in the digital realm, every action leaves a traceable record, and attempts to conceal unethical behavior are often futile in the face of modern forensic tools.

## Human Element and Fallout: The Troy Baker Partnership and Its Demise

The involvement of acclaimed voice actor Troy Baker transformed the Voiceverse scandal from a specialized critique of a crypto startup into a widely reported cultural moment, amplifying its impact and highlighting the precarious position of celebrity endorsers in the volatile world of Web3. On January 14, 2022, Baker announced his partnership with Voiceverse via a social media post that immediately set a confrontational tone , . His message included the inflammatory phrase, "You can hate. Or you can create. What'll it be?" , . This rhetoric framed any skepticism or criticism of NFTs or the Voiceverse project itself as mere "hating," effectively dismissing dissent and creating an adversarial atmosphere before the plagiarism was even revealed . Known for his roles in major video games like *The Last of Us* and various Batman titles, Baker's endorsement lent significant legitimacy to the project, positioning it as a forward-thinking venture aimed at empowering creators in the Metaverse , . However, his choice of words backfired spectacularly in the ensuing media firestorm. The hashtag #hate started trending, and his tweet was widely criticized for its antagonistic and dismissive nature , . The backlash was not limited to anonymous online users; it was echoed by peers in the creative community, including game developers Mike Bithell, Alanah Pearce, and Austin Wintory, who dedicated a segment of their podcast *Play, Watch, Listen* to discussing the controversy with him shortly after his initial announcement .

When the 15.ai exposé broke on the same day as his announcement, the situation escalated rapidly. Facing intense public pressure, Baker reversed his position nine days later. On January 31, 2022, he terminated his partnership with Voiceverse, issuing a formal statement on Twitter , . His retraction was notable for its direct acknowledgment of the failure of his initial communication strategy. He wrote, "Thank you all for your feedback and patience. After careful consideration, I’ve decided to not continue the partnership with VoiceVerseNFT. Intentions aside, I’ve heard you and apologize for accusing anyone of 'hating' just by simply disagreeing with me" . This apology directly addressed the public and peer criticism he had received, showing that the toxic environment fostered by his original tweet was a significant factor in his decision to sever ties . The mutual termination was officially confirmed by both parties. Voiceverse responded with a tweet stating, "We have mutually decided to end our partnership with Troy Baker" . In this statement, the company sought to project an image of resilience, reaffirming its commitment to executing its roadmap and becoming "the voice of Web3.0" . This response starkly contrasted with the reality of the situation: the company had just admitted to a foundational act of theft and was facing widespread condemnation . The dismissal of the partnership served as a final blow to Voiceverse's credibility, signaling to the market that even a high-profile celebrity could not salvage a project built on a foundation of deception. The episode illustrates the double-edged sword of celebrity endorsements in emerging industries; while they can provide a veneer of legitimacy, they also expose individuals to immense personal risk and scrutiny. Baker's experience demonstrates that in the era of instantaneous social media, a single poorly considered statement can become a focal point of failure during a crisis, and that the integrity of a project's leadership ultimately outweighs the value of its celebrity supporters.

## The Ecosystem of Plagiarism: Systemic Issues in Early NFT Marketplaces

The Voiceverse scandal did not occur in a vacuum; it was a prominent symptom of a much larger, systemic crisis of plagiarism and fraud that plagued the early NFT marketplaces in 2022. The brazenness of Voiceverse's actions was enabled by a permissive ecosystem where lax enforcement, user-friendly minting tools, and a general ethos of "move fast and break things" created fertile ground for bad actors. The timing of the Voiceverse incident coincided with a period of unprecedented abuse across the dominant platforms, most notably OpenSea. In January 2022, OpenSea publicly acknowledged the scale of the problem, stating that over 80% of the NFTs created for free on its platform were "plagiarized works, fake collections, and spam" , , , . This staggering statistic revealed that Voiceverse was not an isolated offender but rather a participant in a widespread culture of intellectual property theft . The primary vector for this abuse was the "lazy minting" feature, which allowed users to create NFTs without paying the blockchain gas fees until a sale was made, drastically lowering the barrier to entry for mass-producing counterfeit goods . Artists and rights holders found themselves inundated with unauthorized copies of their work, often finding their creations tokenized and sold by strangers .

In response to the mounting crisis, major NFT marketplaces were forced to take drastic measures, though their solutions were often reactive and imperfect. OpenSea attempted to curb the abuse by announcing a policy limiting free mints to 50 items per user . However, this move was met with significant community backlash and was quickly reversed, highlighting the difficulty platforms faced in balancing anti-fraud efforts with user accessibility . Meanwhile, the marketplace Cent took a more extreme approach. Following reports of rampant unauthorized re-minting of others' work, Cent suspended all NFT sales on February 6, 2022, except for its dedicated "Valuables" marketplace for tweet NFTs , , . CEO Cameron Hejazi described the problem as a "fundamental problem" in Web3 and compared existing enforcement efforts to a "whack-a-mole" game, noting that account bans were unsustainable and temporary measures like free-mint limits had failed , . This admission from a platform that had famously sold Jack Dorsey's first tweet NFT for $2.9 million underscored the fragility of the trust model underpinning the early NFT space .

The failure of centralized platforms to adequately police their marketplaces led to a shift in defensive strategies among artists and communities. Many creators publicly denounced platforms like OpenSea for their slow and inadequate responses to DMCA takedown requests . Prominent artists such as Liam Sharp and RJ Palmer expressed frustration with having to report repeated thefts only to have them ignored . This prompted third-party initiatives to fill the void. DeviantArt, for instance, launched a machine learning tool called 'DeviantArt Protect,' which scans Ethereum and Polygon blockchains for possible infringements, sending over 50,000 alerts since its deployment . The development of such tools highlights a critical gap in the ecosystem: the lack of robust, automated systems for intellectual property protection, a problem that remains unresolved today. The Voiceverse scandal fits squarely within this context. The project's ability to commit such a blatant act of plagiarism so close to its launch, and to use a platform like OpenSea for distribution, was a direct result of the systemic failures of the time. The incident serves as a powerful microcosm of the "Wild West" era of Web3, where technological innovation outpaced the development of governance, legal frameworks, and ethical standards. The fact that a high-profile startup could engage in such egregious behavior with relative impunity speaks volumes about the perceived lack of accountability in an environment where enforcement was weak and tools for copying were ubiquitous. The industry's subsequent struggles to combat this wave of fraud demonstrate that the problems identified during the Voiceverse scandal were not unique to one company, but endemic to the entire digital asset landscape at the time.

## Beyond the Code: Controversies Surrounding the Artist Saba Moeel

While the Voiceverse scandal was primarily defined by its technical act of plagiarism, deeper investigations revealed troubling patterns of misconduct associated with its artist, Saba Moeel, also known by her artistic name Pink Cat. Her involvement with the project brought the focus onto the human element behind the technology, uncovering a history of visual art tracing, cultural appropriation, and problematic online conduct that ultimately led to her condemnation by professional institutions , . The allegations against Moeel went far beyond the scope of the 15.ai incident, painting a picture of an artist accused of systematically misappropriating the work of others for commercial gain. She was accused of tracing copyrighted artwork from well-known properties such as 'Tank Girl' and 'Tom and Jerry', as well as incorporating uncredited artwork from multiple other Instagram artists into her own portfolio . These accusations of "swiping" or tracing artworks—creating derivative works based on another's original creation without permission—escalated the controversy beyond standard NFT-related criticisms like environmental concerns or over-commercialization, shifting the focus to questions of artistic integrity and ethics . The issue gained significant traction within the comics and digital art communities, who pointed to these alleged transgressions as evidence of a pattern of behavior that was unacceptable for a featured guest at a major festival , .

Perhaps the most serious and damaging aspect of the controversy surrounding Moeel involved allegations of the commodification and appropriation of Black culture. Moeel herself identified her alter ego, "Pink Cat," as Black in a 2019 profile . However, she faced sharp criticism for allegedly profiting from this identity while being connected to projects and expressing views seen as harmful to the Black community , . One artist, Ngozi Ukazu, withdrew from the Toronto Comic Arts Festival (TCAF) in protest of Moeel's actions, citing the explicit commodification of Black culture as a primary reason . This accusation moved the debate from a simple question of plagiarism to a more complex discussion about cultural sensitivity, exploitation, and the responsibilities of artists who represent marginalized identities. The combination of visual art tracing and cultural appropriation created a perfect storm of community outrage, leading to sustained calls for accountability.

The collective pressure from the comics community culminated in a swift and decisive institutional response from TCAF. On May 31, 2022, the festival announced that it was rescinding its invitation to Saba Moeel to appear as a featured guest , . In its official statement, TCAF cited "code of conduct violations and the concerns expressed by the comics community," explicitly mentioning "Moeel's online conduct, plagiarism, or allegations of tracing" as the reasons for its decision , . The statement was significant in its candor; TCAF admitted it had been "unaware of Moeel’s online conduct, plagiarism, or allegations of tracing" at the time of the initial invitation and apologized for "programming and promoting this artist" , . The festival's Marketing Manager later confirmed via email that the "online conduct" cited included Moeel's past transphobic tweets from 2016 and 2017, as well as recent responses to criticism from the comics community . TCAF affirmed its zero-tolerance policy for racist or transphobic behavior, making it clear that the decision was a reflection of its institutional values . This case represents a critical dimension of the Voiceverse saga, demonstrating that the reputation of a project can be severely damaged not only by the technical misconduct of its creators but also by the deeply problematic behavior of its associated artists. The condemnation from TCAF signaled a growing intolerance within professional communities for artists who engage in appropriation, plagiarism, and discriminatory speech, regardless of their digital presence or popularity. For Voiceverse, the fallout from Moeel's controversies added another layer of stigma, reinforcing the perception that the project was built on a foundation of questionable ethics.

## Legal Ramifications: Intellectual Property and the Rise of AI Misuse Litigation

The repercussions of the Voiceverse NFT Plagiarism Scandal extended far beyond public relations damage, evolving into a significant legal precedent that reshaped the understanding of intellectual property rights in the age of artificial intelligence. The incident, committed by a subsidiary of LOVO, Inc., provided the evidentiary backbone for a subsequent class-action lawsuit filed against the parent company on September 25, 2024 , . This lawsuit did not merely seek redress for the 2022 theft but aimed to expose what plaintiffs claimed was a "systemic intellectual property theft" culture within LOVO, Inc. , . The legal battle highlighted the complexities of applying traditional copyright law to AI-generated outputs and underscored the power of alternative legal theories, particularly the "right of publicity," in holding corporations accountable for deceptive data acquisition practices. The case against LOVO, Inc. centered on a pattern of fraud that mirrored the tactics used by Voiceverse. Professional voice-over artists Paul Skye Lehrman and Linnea Sage sued the company, alleging that their voices were cloned and sold commercially without their authorization , . The artists discovered their voices were being used as the commercial AI voice clones "Kyle Snow" and "Sally Coleman" on LOVO's Genny text-to-speech platform , . The method of acquisition was identical to the Voiceverse scandal: in 2019–2020, anonymous LOVO employees had hired Lehrman and Sage on the freelance platform Fiverr, promising that their recordings would be used exclusively for "academic research purposes only" and "test scripts for radio ads" with "no external disclosure" , . Instead, LOVO incorporated their recordings into its AI models, trained the system on their unique vocal signatures, and subsequently marketed the resulting clones to subscribers for use in audiobooks, advertisements, and podcasts .

The judicial handling of the lawsuit produced a landmark ruling that clarified the boundaries of liability in AI-driven IP disputes. In a pivotal opinion issued on July 10, 2025, Judge J. Paul Oetken of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York granted in part and denied in part LOVO's motion to dismiss the case , . The court's decision had two critical components. First, it dismissed the federal copyright claims related to the AI-generated voice clones themselves. The judge ruled that under current U.S. law, copyright protects fixed sound recordings and the specific expression within them, but it does not protect abstract qualities like a person's voice or an AI's imitation of it , . This ruling reinforces the principle that works entirely generated by AI without sufficient human authorship are not copyrightable, a doctrine solidified by cases like *Thaler v. Perlmutter* and *Zarya of the Dawn* , . However, the second component of the ruling was far more consequential. The court allowed several state-law claims to proceed, establishing a powerful new avenue for legal challenge , . These surviving claims included:
1. **Breach of Contract:** The court found that LOVO's use of the voice recordings for commercial purposes, in direct contradiction to the promises made on Fiverr, constituted a clear breach of contract , .
2. **Right of Publicity (NY Civil Rights Law §§ 50–51):** The court affirmed that the unauthorized commercial use of recognizable voices constitutes a violation of an individual's right to control the commercial use of their name, image, and likeness , . This claim was bolstered by legal precedents in jurisdictions like California, Tennessee, and New York, which protect distinctive aesthetic signatures and vocal styles from unauthorized commercial use .
3. **New York Consumer Protection Violations (§§ 349–350):** The deceptive practices used to acquire the training data were deemed actionable under state consumer protection statutes , .

This judicial outcome represents a paradigm shift in the fight against AI-driven IP infringement. While the AI clone itself may fall outside the purview of federal copyright law, the deceptive methods used to build the very AI model that produces the clone are now subject to legal challenge. The Voiceverse scandal, with its documented pattern of lying to acquire data, provided the crucial link that allowed plaintiffs in the LOVO case to argue that the company's business model was built on a foundation of fraud. By allowing breach-of-contract and right-of-publicity claims to proceed, the courts have given creators and consumers a potent weapon against companies that exploit AI technology through unethical means. The Voiceverse incident, therefore, transcends its status as a singular act of plagiarism; it became the real-world catalyst that enabled future litigation to establish new legal precedents, forcing the industry to confront the ethical and legal obligations that accompany the development and deployment of generative AI.

The dismissal of the partnership served as a final blow to Voiceverse's credibility.
The dismissal signaled to the market that even a high-profile celebrity could not salvage a project built on a foundation of deception.
The episode illustrates the double-edged sword of celebrity endorsements in emerging industries.
Celebrity endorsements can provide a veneer of legitimacy.
Celebrity endorsements also expose individuals to immense personal risk and scrutiny.
Troy Baker's experience demonstrates that in the era of instantaneous social media, a single poorly considered statement can become a focal point of failure during a crisis.
The integrity of a project's leadership ultimately outweighs the value of its celebrity supporters.
The Voiceverse scandal did not occur in a vacuum.
The Voiceverse scandal was a prominent symptom of a much larger, systemic crisis of plagiarism and fraud that plagued the early NFT marketplaces in 2022.

The brazenness of Voiceverse's actions was enabled by a permissive ecosystem where lax enforcement, user-friendly minting tools, and a general ethos of "move fast and break things" created fertile ground for bad actors.
The timing of the Voiceverse incident coincided with a period of unprecedented abuse across the dominant platforms, most notably OpenSea.
In January 2022, OpenSea publicly acknowledged the scale of the problem.
OpenSea stated that over 80% of the NFTs created for free on its platform were "plagiarized works, fake collections, and spam".
This staggering statistic revealed that Voiceverse was not an isolated offender but rather a participant in a widespread culture of intellectual property theft.

The primary vector for this abuse was the "lazy minting" feature, which allowed users to create NFTs without paying the blockchain gas fees until a sale was made, drastically lowering the barrier to entry for mass-producing counterfeit goods.
Artists and rights holders found themselves inundated with unauthorized copies of their work, often finding their creations tokenized and sold by strangers.
In response to the mounting crisis, major NFT marketplaces were forced to take drastic measures, though their solutions were often reactive and imperfect.
OpenSea attempted to curb the abuse by announcing a policy limiting free mints to 50 items per user.
This move was met with significant community backlash and was quickly reversed, highlighting the difficulty platforms faced in balancing anti-fraud efforts with user accessibility.
Meanwhile, the marketplace Cent took a more extreme approach.
Following reports of rampant unauthorized re-minting of others' work, Cent suspended all NFT sales on February 6, 2022, except for its dedicated "Valuables" marketplace for tweet NFTs.
CEO Cameron Hejazi described the problem as a "fundamental problem" in Web3.
Cameron Hejazi compared existing enforcement efforts to a "whack-a-mole" game.
Cameron Hejazi noted that account bans were unsustainable and temporary measures like free-mint limits had failed.
This admission from a platform that had famously sold Jack Dorsey's first tweet NFT for $2.9 million underscored the fragility of the trust model underpinning the early NFT space.
The failure of centralized platforms to adequately police their marketplaces led to a shift in defensive strategies among artists and communities.
Many creators publicly denounced platforms like OpenSea for their slow and inadequate responses to DMCA takedown requests.
Prominent artists such as Liam Sharp and RJ Palmer expressed frustration with having to report repeated thefts only to have them ignored.
This prompted third-party initiatives to fill the void.
DeviantArt launched a machine learning tool called 'DeviantArt Protect,' which scans Ethereum and Polygon blockchains for possible infringements.
DeviantArt Protect has sent over 50,000 alerts since its deployment.
The development of such tools highlights a critical gap in the ecosystem: the lack of robust, automated systems for intellectual property protection, a problem that remains unresolved today.
The Voiceverse scandal fits squarely within this context.
The project's ability to commit such a blatant act of plagiarism so close to its launch, and to use a platform like OpenSea for distribution, was a direct result of the systemic failures of the time.
The incident serves as a powerful microcosm of the "Wild West" era of Web3, where technological innovation outpaced the development of governance, legal frameworks, and ethical standards.

The fact that a high-profile startup could engage in such egregious behavior with relative impunity speaks volumes about the perceived lack of accountability in an environment where enforcement was weak and tools for copying were ubiquitous.

The industry's subsequent struggles to combat this wave of fraud demonstrate that the problems identified during the Voiceverse scandal were not unique to one company, but endemic to the entire digital asset landscape at the time.

While the Voiceverse scandal was primarily defined by its technical act of plagiarism, deeper investigations revealed troubling patterns of misconduct associated with its artist, Saba Moeel, also known by her artistic name Pink Cat.

Saba Moeel's involvement with the project brought the focus onto the human element behind the technology, uncovering a history of visual art tracing, cultural appropriation, and problematic online conduct that ultimately led to her condemnation by professional institutions.
The allegations against Moeel went far beyond the scope of the 15.ai incident, painting a picture of an artist accused of systematically misappropriating the work of others for commercial gain.
Saba Moeel was accused of tracing copyrighted artwork from well-known properties such as 'Tank Girl' and 'Tom and Jerry'.
Saba Moeel was accused of incorporating uncredited artwork from multiple other Instagram artists into her own portfolio.

These accusations of "swiping" or tracing artworks—creating derivative works based on another's original creation without permission—escalated the controversy beyond standard NFT-related criticisms like environmental concerns or over-commercialization, shifting the focus to questions of artistic integrity and ethics.

The issue gained significant traction within the comics and digital art communities, who pointed to these alleged transgressions as evidence of a pattern of behavior that was unacceptable for a featured guest at a major festival.
The most serious and damaging aspect of the controversy surrounding Moeel involved allegations of the commodification and appropriation of Black culture.
Moeel herself identified her alter ego, "Pink Cat," as Black in a 2019 profile.
Saba Moeel faced sharp criticism for allegedly profiting from this identity while being connected to projects and expressing views seen as harmful to the Black community.
One artist, Ngozi Ukazu, withdrew from the Toronto Comic Arts Festival (TCAF) in protest of Moeel's actions, citing the explicit commodification of Black culture as a primary reason.

This accusation moved the debate from a simple question of plagiarism to a more complex discussion about cultural sensitivity, exploitation, and the responsibilities of artists who represent marginalized identities.
The combination of visual art tracing and cultural appropriation created a perfect storm of community outrage, leading to sustained calls for accountability.
The collective pressure from the comics community culminated in a swift and decisive institutional response from TCAF.
On May 31, 2022, the Toronto Comic Arts Festival (TCAF) announced that it was rescinding its invitation to Saba Moeel to appear as a featured guest.
In its official statement, TCAF cited "code of conduct violations and the concerns expressed by the comics community" as reasons for its decision.
TCAF explicitly mentioned "Moeel’s online conduct, plagiarism, or allegations of tracing" as the reasons for its decision.
The statement was significant in its candor.
TCAF admitted it had been "unaware of Moeel’s online conduct, plagiarism, or allegations of tracing" at the time of the initial invitation.
TCAF apologized for "programming and promoting this artist".

The festival's Marketing Manager later confirmed via email that the "online conduct" cited included Moeel’s past transphobic tweets from 2016 and 2017, as well as recent responses to criticism from the comics community.
TCAF affirmed its zero-tolerance policy for racist or transphobic behavior.
TCAF made it clear that the decision was a reflection of its institutional values.

This case represents a critical dimension of the Voiceverse saga, demonstrating that the reputation of a project can be severely damaged not only by the technical misconduct of its creators but also by the deeply problematic behavior of its associated artists.

The condemnation from TCAF signaled a growing intolerance within professional communities for artists who engage in appropriation, plagiarism, and discriminatory speech, regardless of their digital presence or popularity.
For Voiceverse, the fallout from Moeel's controversies added another layer of stigma, reinforcing the perception that the project was built on a foundation of questionable ethics.

The repercussions of the Voiceverse NFT Plagiarism Scandal extended far beyond public relations damage, evolving into a significant legal precedent that reshaped the understanding of intellectual property rights in the age of artificial intelligence.
The Voiceverse incident, committed by a subsidiary of LOVO, Inc., provided the evidentiary backbone for a subsequent class-action lawsuit filed against the parent company on September 25, 2024.
This lawsuit did not merely seek redress for the 2022 theft but aimed to expose what plaintiffs claimed was a "systemic intellectual property theft" culture within LOVO, Inc.
The legal battle highlighted the complexities of applying traditional copyright law to AI-generated outputs.
The legal battle underscored the power of alternative legal theories, particularly the "right of publicity," in holding corporations accountable for deceptive data acquisition practices.
The case against LOVO, Inc. centered on a pattern of fraud that mirrored the tactics used by Voiceverse.
Professional voice-over artists Paul Skye Lehrman and Linnea Sage sued LOVO, Inc., alleging that their voices were cloned and sold commercially without their authorization.
The artists discovered their voices were being used as the commercial AI voice clones "Kyle Snow" and "Sally Coleman" on LOVO's Genny text-to-speech platform.
The method of acquisition was identical to the Voiceverse scandal.
In 2019–2020, anonymous LOVO employees had hired Lehrman and Sage on the freelance platform Fiverr.
LOVO employees promised that Lehrman and Sage's recordings would be used exclusively for "academic research purposes only" and "test scripts for radio ads" with "no external disclosure".
Instead, LOVO incorporated Lehrman and Sage's recordings into its AI models.
LOVO trained the system on Lehrman and Sage's unique vocal signatures.
LOVO subsequently marketed the resulting clones to subscribers for use in audiobooks, advertisements, and podcasts.
The judicial handling of the lawsuit produced a landmark ruling that clarified the boundaries of liability in AI-driven IP disputes.

In a pivotal opinion issued on July 10, 2025, Judge J. Paul Oetken of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York granted in part and denied in part LOVO's motion to dismiss the case.
The court's decision had two critical components.
First, the court dismissed the federal copyright claims related to the AI-generated voice clones themselves.

The judge ruled that under current U.S. law, copyright protects fixed sound recordings and the specific expression within them, but it does not protect abstract qualities like a person's voice or an AI's imitation of it.
This ruling reinforces the principle that works entirely generated by AI without sufficient human authorship are not copyrightable.
This doctrine was solidified by cases like *Thaler v. Perlmutter* and *Zarya of the Dawn*.
The second component of the ruling was far more consequential.
The court allowed several state-law claims to proceed, establishing a powerful new avenue for legal challenge.
The court found that LOVO's use of the voice recordings for commercial purposes, in direct contradiction to the promises made on Fiverr, constituted a clear breach of contract.
The court affirmed that the unauthorized commercial use of recognizable voices constitutes a violation of an individual's right to control the commercial use of their name, image, and likeness.

This claim was bolstered by legal precedents in jurisdictions like California, Tennessee, and New York, which protect distinctive aesthetic signatures and vocal styles from unauthorized commercial use.
The deceptive practices used to acquire the training data were deemed actionable under state consumer protection statutes.
This judicial outcome represents a paradigm shift in the fight against AI-driven IP infringement.
While the AI clone itself may fall outside the purview of federal copyright law, the deceptive methods used to build the very AI model that produces the clone are now subject to legal challenge.

The Voiceverse scandal, with its documented pattern of lying to acquire data, provided the crucial link that allowed plaintiffs in the LOVO case to argue that the company's business model was built on a foundation of fraud.

By allowing breach-of-contract and right-of-publicity claims to proceed, the courts have given creators and consumers a potent weapon against companies that exploit AI technology through unethical means.
The Voiceverse incident transcends its status as a singular act of plagiarism.

The Voiceverse incident became the real-world catalyst that enabled future litigation to establish new legal precedents, forcing the industry to confront the ethical and legal obligations that accompany the development and deployment of generative AI.

AI Twins and Avatars: Legal Risks for Companies Using Synthetic Voice and Likeness Technology 
==============================================================================================

**by [Traverse Legal](https://www.traverselegal.com/)[,](https://www.traverselegal.com/enrico-schaefer/) reviewed by [Enrico Schaefer](https://www.traverselegal.com/enrico-schaefer/)** - May 1, 2025 - [Ai Tips For Lawyers](https://www.traverselegal.com/blog/category/ai-tips-for-lawyers/), [Artificial Intelligence](https://www.traverselegal.com/blog/category/artificial-intelligence/), [Copyright Infringement on the Internet](https://www.traverselegal.com/blog/category/copyright/copyright-infringement-on-the-internet/), [Copyright Law](https://www.traverselegal.com/blog/category/copyright/)

###### Share This:

[Pinterest](https://www.traverselegal.com/blog/ai-avatar-legal-risks/#)[X](https://www.traverselegal.com/blog/ai-avatar-legal-risks/#)[Facebook](https://www.traverselegal.com/blog/ai-avatar-legal-risks/#)[Google+](https://www.traverselegal.com/blog/ai-avatar-legal-risks/#)[Email](mailto:?subject=AI%20Twins%20and%20Avatars%3A%20Legal%20Risks%20for%20Companies%20Using%20Synthetic%20Voice%20and%20Likeness%20Technology%C2%A0&body=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.traverselegal.com%2Fblog%2Fai-avatar-legal-risks%2F)

![Image 2: img](https://www.traverselegal.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/AI-Avatar-Depiction.jpg)

The rapid advancement of AI-generated avatars, commonly referred to as “AI twins” is transforming how businesses delegate tasks, interact with customers, and scale their brand. A founder can now deploy a digital version of themselves to attend meetings, pitch investors, or onboard users without ever hitting “join” on a Zoom call. Enterprise teams are experimenting with synthetic voice assistants that sound eerily like trusted public figures. And entire product demos can now be delivered by virtual replicas of real employees.

But behind the convenience of outsourcing human presence lies a growing thicket of legal exposure. As more startups and companies deploy AI likenesses; whether based on internal team members, hired talent, or public figures the question isn’t if there are risks. It’s how big, how complex, and how avoidable they are.

This article unpacks the core legal issues AI companies must address when using synthetic representations of real people. From copyright to publicity rights, the risks are real, and the time to address them is now.

**Who Owns the Work Created by AI Twins?** 
-------------------------------------------

This is one of the most fundamental (and frequently misunderstood) issues facing AI companies today. Under U.S. copyright law, creative works must be authored by a human to receive protection. If an AI twin generates a training video, records a podcast episode, or even delivers a sales pitch, can that output be copyrighted? And if so, by whom?

If a human is behind the script, but the avatar delivers it, that’s one layer. If the AI twin improvises, adapts, or performs content in a way that mimics human creativity, courts may view that differently.  Current U.S. Copyright Office guidance (and caselaw like [Thaler v. Perlmutter](https://media.cadc.uscourts.gov/opinions/docs/2025/03/23-5233.pdf)) confirms that non-human-generated content is not copyrightable. There must be a human element of authorship—whether in scripting, direction, or creative input.Either way, the company using the avatar must be clear on ownership; not just of the likeness, but of what the avatar produces.

Now consider a common scenario: your company licenses a digital likeness from a creator or influencer, then uses that AI twin to generate customer-facing content. While you may own the _deliverables_, you might not own the underlying likeness; or the legal rights to continue using the outputs if that license ends. Things get even murkier when models or voice data are licensed from third-party providers without clear downstream usage terms.  That’s why relying on default copyright rules isn’t enough. Companies must proactively set the terms.

**Key takeaway:** Contracts are not just a formality. They’re your primary defense. Agreements with both developers (who build or train the AI twin) and talent (whose likeness or voice is being used) should explicitly assign copyright rights, cover derivative works, and define exactly who owns the outputs—now and in the future.

**Publicity Rights & Likeness Use** 
------------------------------------

One of the most immediate legal risks of using AI avatars is violating a person’s right of publicity. The legal right to control how one’s name, image, voice, or likeness is used for commercial purposes.

Unlike copyright, the right of publicity is governed by state law. That means protections vary widely, but in many states, this right extends beyond just celebrities. Employees, creators, influencers, and even private individuals may have a claim if their likeness is used in a product without their permission.

This matters deeply in the context of AI twins. If you create a digital avatar that looks or sounds like a real person. Even if generated or altered using AI, you may be held liable if that person didn’t give express permission. Courts have shown that even “transformative” outputs, like stylized or AI-modified representations, may still infringe on [publicity rights](https://www.traverselegal.com/blog/are-your-publicity-rights-protected-for-the-ai-surge/) if they evoke a recognizable identity.

Take, for example, a startup that trains its AI assistant to sound like a well-known actor or athlete. Even if the output is novel or altered for a comedic app, that’s not a free pass. Parody, innovation, or artistic intent don’t override commercial misappropriation. Legal battles around deepfakes, influencer cloning, and unauthorized voice synthesis are already testing these boundaries.

**What should companies do?** Get ahead of the risk before a model is trained or an avatar is deployed.

A well-drafted publicity release is critical. It should go beyond basic image use and include clear rights for:

*   AI training and dataset inclusion 

*   Derivative works and modified outputs 

*   Future and posthumous use, especially if the avatar may be used after a contract ends or a creator passes away 

Also, don’t treat publicity rights as one-size-fits-all. States like California, Tennessee, and New York have some of the strongest protections, including post-mortem rights that can last for decades. If you’re building a product used nationwide, or training models on a wide range of individuals, state-by-state compliance isn’t optional.

**The bottom line:** Consent isn’t a checkbox. It’s a shield. Companies that rely on AI likenesses must treat publicity rights as core infrastructure, and not as an afterthought.

**Voice Imitation and Synthetic Speech Risks** 
-----------------------------------------------

Synthetic voice is one of the most compelling and legally risky areas in the AI likeness space. If your AI-generated voice sounds too much like a real person, you may be entering dangerous territory.

When an AI mimics a specific voice pattern or tone, especially that of a recognizable figure, it can trigger claims of “voice theft,” misappropriation, or even false endorsement. And unlike a generic avatar, voice is deeply tied to identity. Courts have recognized that a voice can be as distinctive and legally protected as a face.

Even if you don’t name the person being imitated, if the voice is clearly evocative of a public figure, or if users are led to believe a real person was involved, that’s where the legal risk sharpens.

This isn’t just a theoretical concern. The **Federal Trade Commission (FTC)** has already signaled that [misleading use of AI-generated content](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2025/04/ftc-order-requires-workado-back-artificial-intelligence-detection-claims), including synthetic voices, could fall under deceptive marketing practices. If an AI voice implies that a celebrity or influencer endorses your product when they don’t, the FTC may step in, and the penalties can be severe.

**So how can companies stay compliant?** Two practical steps make a major difference.

First, always disclose when a voice is synthetic. If users believe they’re hearing a real person or worse, a real endorsement, you’re walking a legal tightrope. Clear, accessible disclosures (especially in ads or customer-facing experiences) help reduce risk.

Second, keep a documented audit trail. You should be able to show how the voice model was created, what data was used, and that any real human contributors gave informed, written consent. This is especially important if you’re using contractors, third-party voice libraries, or open-source models trained on scraped content.

Without those safeguards, even unintentional voice imitation can escalate into a legal challenge, one that’s harder to defend after the fact.

**Licensing Agreements for Likeness, Voice, and Personality** 
--------------------------------------------------------------

When you’re building AI avatars or using real people’s voices and likenesses, contracts aren’t just paperwork; they’re your legal backbone. A strong licensing agreement doesn’t just protect you from future disputes; it gives your product the green light to scale responsibly.

At minimum, your contracts should spell out the duration, territory, and scope of use. That means getting specific: Are you using the likeness for training only, or will it also power customer-facing experiences? Is the usage global or limited to a certain market? Will content be used in ads, internal tools, or both?

Then there’s the matter of exclusivity. Are you the only one who can use the person’s AI likeness, or are they free to license it to others? This becomes a business differentiator when talent likeness becomes a brand asset.

Equally important is what happens after the agreement ends. A well-structured contract should include revocability clauses and post-use obligations, like requiring the company to take down AI-generated content or deactivate avatars built using the licensed data. Without this, companies risk dragging legal baggage into future product cycles, or worse, into court.

One emerging best practice especially for companies operating internationally, is including a moral rights clause. U.S. law doesn’t formally recognize “moral rights” for likeness or voice, especially in the way other jurisdictions like the EU do. But that doesn’t mean they should be ignored. In practice, moral rights clauses serve a different function: they build trust with talent, signal respect for creators, and anticipate reputational concerns that could spiral into disputes later. Even if unenforceable under U.S. copyright law, these clauses send a message—you’re thinking ahead, not just legally, ethically, and relationally. And for global companies, or those working with international creators, moral rights protections aren’t optional. They’re the price of admission.  For example, an artist may object to their AI twin being used in ways that conflict with their values or reputation.

Including such clauses signals respect for the human behind the likeness, and increasingly, it’s what talent, influencers, and creators are asking for. It’s also a sign to regulators and the public that your company is thinking ahead.

Bottom line: Licensing agreements are no longer one-page releases. In the AI era, they need to be structured for nuance, consent, and change.

**What Talent Should Know Before Lending Their Voice or Image** 
----------------------------------------------------------------

For creators, influencers, voice actors, and even everyday professionals, the idea of having your own AI twin can be exciting, and potentially lucrative. But the legal and reputational risks are real. Once your likeness or voice is digitized and integrated into a product, it can take on a life of its own.

Before signing away rights to your identity, it’s worth slowing down and asking a few critical questions.

### **Can the avatar say things I don’t agree with?**

Unless your contract sets limits, the answer could be yes. Without guardrails, your AI twin might one day promote products, causes, or viewpoints that conflict with your values—or worse, harm your reputation.

### **Can the company sell or license my voice/image to others?**

If the agreement allows sub-licensing or model reuse, your voice or likeness could end up in products you’ve never heard of, let alone approved. Control over downstream use is one of the most overlooked clauses in AI likeness deals.

### **Will I be paid ongoing royalties, or just a one-time fee?**

Make sure compensation reflects the scope and lifespan of the license. A flat fee may not be fair if your avatar is being used at scale, in multiple markets, or generating significant revenue for the company.

To protect yourself, negotiate specific use limitations. For example, banning political content, adult content, or any context that feels out of alignment with your personal or professional brand. You can also push for periodic reviews or even opt-out clauses that allow you to revoke permission under certain conditions.

Lastly, always ask for indemnification. If your likeness is used in a way that misleads users, spreads false endorsements, or damages your reputation, you shouldn’t be left holding the bag. A solid indemnity clause ensures the company using your avatar is also responsible for keeping it in line.

For talent, these conversations may feel new, but they’re becoming essential. As AI twins become more common, so too will the need for smart, protective contracts that honor both the human and the technology.

**Regulatory Landscape and What’s Coming** 
-------------------------------------------

The legal framework around AI avatars and synthetic voice is still forming, but it’s evolving fast. On the state level, several laws already hint at where regulation is headed. California’s AB 730 prohibits the use of deepfakes or synthetic media in political ads within 60 days of an election. This law marks one of the first state-level responses to AI-generated likeness abuse.

Meanwhile, Illinois’ Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) remains one of the strongest in the country. It requires consent before collecting or using biometric identifiers like voiceprints or facial scans. BIPA has already been used in high-profile cases against major tech companies, and AI startups should take note.

At the federal level, momentum is building around both right-of-publicity reform and FTC scrutiny of deceptive synthetic media. The FTC has warned that AI-generated endorsements, voices, or representations, if not properly disclosed, could qualify as unfair or deceptive under existing advertising laws. The FTC can issue fines under Section 5 of the FTC Act and enforce civil penalties for noncompliance. Mentioning this would further underscore the seriousness of synthetic voice misuse.

What does this mean for companies building or deploying AI twins? The window for operating in a legal gray zone is closing. Compliance, transparency, and strong contracts aren’t just best practices anymore. They’re fast becoming baseline expectations.

Data Use & Privacy
------------------

Don’t overlook the training data. It’s one of the most common blind spots we see with AI companies, especially fast-moving teams racing to ship features. Pulling voice samples, facial scans, or likeness data from scraped sources or user uploads might already be crossing legal lines under laws like the CCPA, GDPR, or even fundamental contract law. Just because data is publicly available doesn’t mean it’s fair game. And if your training set includes minors—even accidentally—you could trigger COPPA restrictions, which come with severe penalties.

This isn’t just a checkbox issue. Training data governance is quickly becoming a cornerstone of AI compliance. You need to know what went into the model, who owns it, and whether consent was ever part of the picture. The FTC, state AGs, and European regulators are all watching this space. Startups that get ahead of this—by documenting sources, securing rights, and building with permission—will have a real advantage when scrutiny hits.

**Make Sure Your AI Twin Has a Legal Backbone** 
------------------------------------------------

AI twins, avatars, and synthetic voices are no longer experimental. They’re powering real products, real interactions, and real revenue. But with that scale comes a real need for legal structure. The laws around digital likeness are still catching up, but the risks are already here.

[![Image 1: This is a good article. Click here for more information.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/94/Symbol_support_vote.svg/20px-Symbol_support_vote.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Good_articles* "This is a good article. Click here for more information.")

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/15chill.png/330px-15chill.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:15chill.png)

[15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15_/(programmer/) "15 (programmer)") ([ponysona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ponysona "Ponysona") pictured) discovered that Voiceverse had used [15.ai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15.ai "15.ai") to generate voice lines that were used to market Voiceverse's partnership with [Troy Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troy_Baker "Troy Baker") and subsequently sold as [NFTs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFT "NFT").

In January 2022, [15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15_/(programmer/) "15 (programmer)")—the pseudonymous [Massachusetts Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "Massachusetts Institute of Technology") (MIT) artificial intelligence researcher and creator of the non-commercial [generative artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence "Generative artificial intelligence") [voice synthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voice_synthesis "Voice synthesis") research project [15.ai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15.ai "15.ai")—discovered that the [blockchain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blockchain "Blockchain")\-based technology company **Voiceverse** had [plagiarized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plagiarism "Plagiarism") from their platform. Voiceverse marketed itself as a service that offered [AI voice cloning technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_deepfake "Audio deepfake") that could be purchased and traded as [non-fungible tokens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-fungible_token "Non-fungible token") (NFTs).

Amid heightened controversy over NFTs in the gaming industry, voice actor [Troy Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troy_Baker "Troy Baker") (who has been described as one of the most famous [voice actors in video games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voice_acting#Voice_acting_in_video_games "Voice acting")) announced his partnership with Voiceverse on January 14, 2022, triggering immediate backlash over concerns about the [environmental impact of NFTs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-fungible_token#Environmental_concerns "Non-fungible token"), [potential for fraud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-fungible_token#Plagiarism_and_fraud "Non-fungible token"), [predatory monetization in video games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_monetization#Criticism "Video game monetization"), and the potential of [AI displacing jobs for human voice actors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technological_unemployment "Technological unemployment"). Later that same day, 15 revealed through server logs that Voiceverse had generated voice lines using 15's free [text-to-speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Text-to-speech "Text-to-speech") platform, pitch-shifted the audio to make them unrecognizable, and [falsely marketed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_advertising "False advertising") the samples as their own technology before selling them as NFTs. Within an hour of being confronted with evidence, Voiceverse confessed and stated that their marketing team had used 15.ai without proper attribution while rushing to create a [technology demo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technology_demo "Technology demo") to coincide with Baker's partnership announcement, further exacerbating the already negative reception to the original announcement. In response, 15 replied "Go fuck yourself"; the interaction went [viral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viral_phenomenon "Viral phenomenon") and garnered a large amount of support for the developer. News publications universally characterized this incident as Voiceverse having "[stolen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theft "Theft")" from 15.ai.

The next day, Baker appeared on a [podcast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast "Podcast") and stated that his motivation had been to help independent creators who were unable to afford professional voice actors. Following continued backlash and the plagiarism revelation, Baker ended his partnership with Voiceverse on January 31, 2022. Subsequently, the incident was documented in multiple [AI ethics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_ethics "AI ethics") databases, criticisms of predatory monetization in video games, and [retrospectives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retrospective "Retrospective") as one of the earliest instances of plagiarism and theft stemming from artificial intelligence during the [AI boom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_boom "AI boom").

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Troy_Baker_%2853616263785%29.jpg/250px-Troy_Baker_%2853616263785%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Troy_Baker_/(53616263785/).jpg)

[Troy Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troy_Baker "Troy Baker") in 2024

[Troy Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troy_Baker "Troy Baker") is a prominent [voice actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voice_actor "Voice actor") in the [video game industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_industry "Video game industry") best known for his performances as [Joel Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joel_/(The_Last_of_Us/) "Joel (The Last of Us)") in [_The Last of Us_ franchise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_of_Us_/(franchise/) "The Last of Us (franchise)").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-Peters-2022-1) Baker has been described as "ubiquitous" by _[Polygon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygon_/(website/) "Polygon (website)")_,[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-McWhertor-2022-2) "one of the most high-profile and prolific voice actors in video games" by _[Eurogamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurogamer "Eurogamer")_,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-Phillips-2022-3) and "arguably the most famous voice actor in the gaming industry" by _GameGuru_.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-Kuchkanov-2022-4) His other prominent roles include voicing Agent John "Jonesy" Jones in _[Fortnite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortnite "Fortnite")_, [Booker DeWitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Booker_DeWitt "Booker DeWitt") in _[BioShock Infinite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BioShock_Infinite "BioShock Infinite")_, and both [Batman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batman "Batman") and [Joker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joker_/(character/) "Joker (character)") in multiple Batman video games.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-McWhertor-2022-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-Phillips-2022-3) As of October 2025, Baker holds the record for the most acting nominations at the [BAFTA Games Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Games_Awards "BAFTA Games Awards"), with five between 2013 and 2021.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-5)

Voiceverse is a [blockchain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blockchain "Blockchain")\-based startup founded by the [Bored Ape Yacht Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bored_Ape_Yacht_Club "Bored Ape Yacht Club")[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-McKean-2022-6) that marketed itself as offering AI voice cloning technology in the form of [NFTs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFT "NFT").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-Makuch-2022-7) Prior to the announcement of their partnership with Baker, Voiceverse had partnered with LOVO, Inc., an AI voice platform that, according to LOVO, could generate human-like voices.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-McWhertor-2022-2) Voiceverse stated that any user who purchases a voice NFT would have unlimited and perpetual access to the voice model,[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-McWhertor-2022-2) which could be used to create content such as [audiobooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audiobook "Audiobook"), [YouTube videos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube_video "YouTube video"), [podcasts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast "Podcast"), e-learning materials, in-game [voice chat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voice_chat "Voice chat"), and [Zoom calls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoom_call "Zoom call").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-Phillips-2022-3)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-Makuch-2022-7) Voiceverse promised that buyers would "OWN _[\[sic\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sic "Sic")_ all of the [IP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intellectual_property "Intellectual property")" of content they created using these voices.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-McWhertor-2022-2) Voiceverse's roadmap included plans to release 8,888 initial voice NFTs, a feature to add emotions to existing voices, and the ability for users to mint their own voices as NFTs. Prior to Baker's partnership, Voiceverse had also partnered with voice actors [Charlet Chung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlet_Chung "Charlet Chung"), who voices [D.Va](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D.Va "D.Va") in _[Overwatch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overwatch "Overwatch")_,[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-McWhertor-2022-2) and [Andy Milonakis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Milonakis "Andy Milonakis") of _[The Andy Milonakis Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Andy_Milonakis_Show "The Andy Milonakis Show")_.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-McWhertor-2022-2)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-Makuch-2022-7)

[15.ai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15.ai "15.ai") is a free web application launched in 2020 that uses [artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence") to generate [text-to-speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Text-to-speech "Text-to-speech") voices of fictional characters from [popular media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_media "Popular media").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-8) Created by a [pseudonymous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudonym "Pseudonym") artificial intelligence researcher known as [15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15_/(programmer/) "15 (programmer)"), who began developing the technology as a [freshman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freshman "Freshman") during their undergraduate research at [MIT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIT "MIT"), it was an early example of an application of [generative artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence "Generative artificial intelligence") during the initial stages of the [AI boom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_boom "AI boom"). The platform showed that [deep neural networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_neural_networks "Deep neural networks") could generate emotionally expressive speech with only 15 seconds of speech; the name "15.ai" references the creator's statement that a voice can be convincingly cloned with just 15 seconds of audio, as opposed to the tens of hours of data previously required. 15.ai became an [Internet phenomenon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_phenomenon "Internet phenomenon") in early 2021 when content utilizing it went viral on [social media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_media "Social media") and quickly gained widespread use among various [Internet fandoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fandom "Fandom"). 15 has emphasized that it remain free and non-commercial; it only requires users to give proper credit when using the service for content creation.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-9)

### NFTs in the video game industry

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: NFTs in the video game industry")\]

By early 2022, NFTs had become highly controversial within the gaming industry.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-McKean-2022-6) Critics raised concerns about their environmental impact due to the significant energy consumption of blockchain technology.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-McKean-2022-6) In addition, the prevalence of scams, fraud, and potential [money laundering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Money_laundering "Money laundering") associated with NFT sales, as well as fears that NFTs were a new form of [predatory monetization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_monetization#Criticism "Video game monetization") following the increasing frequency of [loot boxes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loot_boxes "Loot boxes"), caused vocal pushback from the gaming community.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-McKean-2022-6) Several major gaming companies had begun exploring NFT integration into their products, though fan backlash had already forced some projects to be cancelled.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-Bankhurst-2022-10) On December 16, 2021,[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-11) the developers of _[S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2: Heart of Chernobyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S.T.A.L.K.E.R._2:_Heart_of_Chernobyl "S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2: Heart of Chernobyl")_ announced that they would be including NFTs in the game, but cancelled within an hour of the announcement due to immediate universal backlash.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-Bankhurst-2022-10)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-Peters-2022-1) Simultaneously, the rise of AI voice technology raised concerns among voice actors about potential job displacement and the devaluation of their work amidst the voice acting industry's ongoing struggles for better compensation and working conditions.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-McKean-2022-6)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-Brown-2022-12)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-McWhertor-2022-2)

Partnership announcement and backlash
-------------------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Partnership announcement and backlash")\]

On January 14, 2022, 1:02 a.m. [EST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Standard_Time "Eastern Standard Time"), Baker announced on [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter") that he was partnering with Voiceverse "to explore ways where together we might bring new tools to new creators to make new things, and allow everyone a chance to own & invest in the IP's they create." The announcement concluded with the statement "You can hate. Or you can create."[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-McWhertor-2022-2)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-Brown-2022-12) Baker's specific role with Voiceverse remained unclear at the time of the announcement.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-McWhertor-2022-2)

A Chubbiverse [promo video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Promo_video "Promo video") posted by Voiceverse. Server logs later showed that the voices were actually generated using [15.ai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15.ai "15.ai") and had been distorted to sound unrecognizable.

Along with Baker's announcement, Voiceverse promoted their supposed voice AI technology on Twitter by posting animated videos that featured a cat character created by NFT firm **Chubbiverse**.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-Phillips-2022-2-13)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-Innes-2022-14) The videos concluded with text that read "The Voice Powered By Voiceverse"; Voiceverse stated on Twitter that the voices in the animations had been generated using their own AI voice synthesis technology and presented the videos as a [technology demonstration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technology_demonstration "Technology demonstration") of their voice NFT capabilities.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-Phillips-2022-2-13)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-Innes-2022-14)

The announcement provoked immediate and widespread backlash from the gaming community.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-McWhertor-2022-2) Baker's tweet received thousands of replies and [quote retweets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tweet_/(social_media/)#Retweets "Tweet (social media)") (the vast majority of which were negative),[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-McWhertor-2022-2) far more than the number of [likes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upvote "Upvote");[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-Bankhurst-2022-10) Michael McWhertor of _Polygon_ described it as a "textbook example of being [ratioed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratioed "Ratioed")" and commented that reactions had been amplified by the final part of Baker's announcement.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-McWhertor-2022-2) Michael Beckwith of _[Metro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_/(UK/) "Metro (UK)")_ called Baker's approach "bizarrely aggressive".[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-Beckwith-2022-15)

Later that day, Baker responded to the backlash by apologizing for his choice of words.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-Bankhurst-2022-10) He said he appreciated people's thoughts and acknowledged that the "hate/create part might have been a bit antagonistic," calling it a "bad attempt to bring levity".[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-Bankhurst-2022-10) Despite the apology, Baker and his fellow voice actors did not distance themselves from Voiceverse at this point.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-McWhertor-2022-2) At the same time, Voiceverse attempted to address the criticisms, stating that they were working to move to more environmentally friendly blockchain technology and that voice actors would receive royalties from NFT sales, with actors benefiting from any increase in NFT value.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal#cite_note-McWhertor-2022-2)

Plagiarism revelation
---------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Voiceverse_NFT_plagiarism_scandal&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Plagiarism revelation")\]
